extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history and general readers interested in 19th‑century American press development
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and frames the quality, legal, operational and social standards implied in a historical account of early‑19th‑century American newspapers (western expansion, abolitionist press, postal censorship, community role). Useful for assessing how newspapers were produced, sustained, and judged in that era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the press / free speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A vigorous advocacy of a free press and the right to public discussion; resistance to any effort to throttle or muzzle newspapers or writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page examples and language: editors like Charles Hammond 'a vigorous advocate of a free press' argued that demands to muzzle abolition editors were an attack on freedom of the press; Hammond 're-asserted the right of freedom of speech and of the press' in defense of James G. Birney. The text shows legal and extra‑legal pressures (legislative proposals, mob action) that threatened this freedom, and treats defense of press freedom as a central standard for good journalism in the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed in gathering and printing news so that public debate and action can be informed in a timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that 'not a word of' the Webster-Hayne debate appeared in Washington journals for two weeks and a month elapsed before Philadelphia papers printed it; that 'this slowness in printing news' led to the introduction of faster newspapers (e.g., Bennett and Greeley). Example: President Monroe's message arriving months late to frontier papers—delays undermined usefulness and spurred new journalistic ventures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper as essential community institution
rubrics_metrics.description: A weekly newspaper was considered necessary for a functioning community and town identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states that in newly settled places (e.g., Mt. Pleasant, Vevay, Indianapolis) the presence of a weekly newspaper was 'without which no community ... was complete' and that towns offered inducements to printers. This functions as a normative expectation: founding a town almost invariably included establishing a paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation as political and social power
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper's influence derives from its circulation and its ability to reach broad publics (including non‑voters), making circulation a key measure of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'The paper with the large circulation was a power in the community, and it derived its power, not from the influential but from the non-voters.' The text cites 1835 statistics (e.g., Missouri's seventeen papers with annual circulation of 720,000) to show circulation as an index of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisanship and political alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers often served as party organs or political advocates; political alignment and engagement were fundamental features of many papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ohio Federalist, Federalist/Gazette, Whig and Democratic party papers, anti‑Masonic organs like Albany Journal, labor and reform papers. The text treats partisan affiliation and active engagement in political debates (e.g., Webster–Hayne, anti‑Masonic movement) as characteristic standards for newspapers of the era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial courage and advocacy (crusading journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Willingness to take controversial moral or political positions and to sustain reform campaigns despite social, legal, or physical threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by abolitionist publishers (Benjamin Lundy, William Lloyd Garrison, James G. Birney) and labor/reform papers (Workingman's Gazette). Guidance implied: strong journalism may require moral courage—Birney printed demands and evidence showing threats to free speech; Lovejoy and Birney endured mob violence and even murder as consequences of advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel law and truth defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal environment: the availability of truth as a defense in libel suits strengthens press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that in Mississippi, Connecticut and New York 'legislation was passed admitting, in libel suits, a defense on the ground of the truth of the allegation.' This legal standard is presented as an important protection for newspapers engaging in robust public discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal/distribution infrastructure and censorship risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependence on the post office and other distribution channels creates vulnerability to official non‑delivery or censorship; control of mail can be used to suppress views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jackson administration's Postmaster-General countenanced non-delivery of abolitionist northern newspapers; proposals (and a committee bill) to prohibit circulation of 'incendiary publications' in the southern states via the mail. The guidance stresses that governmental control of distribution is a critical structural criterion affecting press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial/operational viability and local economic support
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers' survival relied on varied payment methods, local inducements, and itinerant printers; economic arrangements shape production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practices cited include subscriptions 'payable in flour, corn, beef or pork', towns offering inducements to printers, and the itinerant class of journeyman printers finding work as settlements grew. These operational realities are presented as necessary conditions for producing and sustaining newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial competence, scholarship, and quality of argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual ability, scholarship, and legal/constitutional knowledge of editors affect the character and authority of a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charles Hammond is praised for 'ability, scholarship, and intellect' and for arguing 'on great questions of constitutional law' in his editorial columns; such qualities are treated as standards that improve a paper's influence and respectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language inclusivity / tailoring to local linguistic audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in appropriate languages or bilingual formats to serve the actual readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In what is now Michigan the first newspaper (1809) was printed 'in French and English.' The criterion suggests matching language to community composition as a production standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to population growth and local demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid founding of newspapers in newly settled or rapidly growing communities demonstrates responsiveness to civic information needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages describing Vevay, Indianapolis and Mt. Pleasant show papers appearing quickly as population and commercial life expanded; responsiveness to local demand is an implicit production/evaluation metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical security and protection of presses
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical need to protect presses, type and printers from mob violence and destruction; physical vulnerability is a production and survival concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple incidents cited: presses smashed in Cincinnati, Alton and St. Louis; Lovejoy's press destroyed repeatedly and he was ultimately murdered defending it. The historical lessons imply that safeguarding physical assets and personnel is a necessary (if not aesthetic) criterion for sustaining journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the press in promoting democratic participation and suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: Press activity that educates, mobilizes, or amplifies the voice of new voter constituencies (non‑propertied men) is seen as central to democratic development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that the extension of manhood suffrage was 'an inevitable result of the assumption of political power by the press' and that the press broke down privileged classes. Thus, an important measure of a paper's civic value is its contribution to broader political participation.
